title: The Hill in Kampala: Makerere, Margaret Trowell and the making of East African modernism
standfirst: A British art teacher's informal classes in Kampala became the training ground for a generation of East African painters and sculptors. The school's legacy is large, and so are the arguments about how it taught.
bodyMarkdown:
Many of the artists who appear in the history of modern art in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania share a single point of origin: the art school at Makerere in Kampala. Sam Ntiro, Gregory Maloba, Elimo Njau, Asaph Ng'ethe Macua, Theresa Musoke, Peter Mulindwa and Kefa Sempangi all studied or taught there. Their paths then fanned out across the region, to Nairobi, Dar es Salaam and back to Kampala, carrying a set of ideas about what a modern East African art might be. This essay traces how the school began, what it taught, and why its legacy is still debated.

## An informal beginning

Margaret Trowell was born in London in 1904 and trained at the Slade School of Fine Art. According to Wikipedia's account of her life, her husband, a physician, was appointed to the Colonial Medical Service, which took the couple to Kenya in 1929 and to Uganda in 1935. In Kenya she lived among the Akamba and wrote about their arts and crafts. The Short Century, a research project of the East African Art and Museum Network, quotes her recollection of that period: "In Kenya (1929-1935), I never saw or heard of any African who was taught art in schools."

The dates of the school's founding vary by source, and the difference is instructive. Asaph Ng'ethe Macua, who studied there, recalls in his autobiography that it "started very casually in 1937 at the house of Margaret Trowell," where people from nearby Mulago Hospital and Makerere students on other courses came to watch her paint and learn. He writes that the classes grew into a School of Art once Trowell "convinced the Principle of Makerere College to include Art among the courses taught at the College," and that it "opened in 1940." Wikipedia gives 1937 as the year she established the Margaret Trowell School of Industrial and Fine Art. Both are accurate in their way: 1937 marks the start of the classes, 1940 the school's formal opening.

The school's footing was never secure. The art historian Sunanda K. Sanyal, quoted on The Short Century, writes that when Makerere became a University College in 1949 "no one had any clear idea how art would fit into a curriculum primarily geared toward training future civil servants," and that art education nearly ended altogether. In her words, it "survived primarily due to the commitment and perseverance of Margaret Trowell." Trowell led the school until her retirement in 1958.

## What was taught

Trowell's method came out of her own training. She studied under Marion Richardson, an English art educator who replaced object drawing with exercises built on the pupil's mental imagery. The Short Century describes how Trowell began each class by delivering "a carefully prepared description of a scene, or a poem or story," and asked students to close their eyes and picture it before drawing. She rarely demonstrated technique or pointed to other artists' work, so the starting point was the student's own imagination.

She also rejected the hierarchy that separated fine art from craft. Her view, as the same source quotes it, was that this distinction was false, and she saw in local textiles and sculpture what she called a "sense of design" on which students could build. Macua remembered her teaching in these terms: "She believed we should use our own local cultures for our inspiration... she encouraged us to bring our indigenous materials to work with and produce our own African ideas of beauty."

The approach was admired and has since been criticised. The Short Century notes that Trowell kept her students away from the modern art of Europe, and describes her as sharing the colonial assumptions of her time about the people she taught. The scholar Emma Wolukau-Wanambwa, whose research it draws on, argues that her model rested on an idea of Africans as unspoiled by modernity. One result, on that reading, was a school that encouraged individuality while limiting students' access to the wider history of art. Trowell discouraged Gregory Maloba's attraction to the Catholic imagery he had grown up with, according to the same account.

## A school of individuals

The artists who emerged were not alike. The critic John Roberts, writing in 1967 and quoted by The Short Century, compared three of them: Njau tended "to a semi-mystical expressionism," Eli Kyeyune made "bold and incisive statements about the appearance of things," and Ng'ethe painted "in dark, almost drab browns a harsh and grinding world." Roberts concluded that it was "impossible to point to any quality in their work and claim that it links them."

Their careers were equally varied. Sam Joseph Ntiro, born in the Kilimanjaro region in 1923, studied at Makerere from 1944 to 1947, according to the Museum of Modern Art's online journal. NCAI's exhibition notes say he later taught painting there from 1948 and attended the Slade between 1952 and 1955. In 1960 the Museum of Modern Art, New York, acquired his painting of men taking banana beer to a bride by night, which made him the first African artist in its collection. Elimo Njau, born in Tanzania in 1932, painted the Murang'a cathedral murals in 1959 and went on to found cultural institutions in Nairobi, a story told in a companion essay. Theresa Musoke, who was among the first women to earn a fine art degree at Makerere, lived in Nairobi from 1974 to 1996 and taught at Kenyatta University and the International School of Kenya, according to the biography prepared for NCAI.

The Short Century also records a sense of belonging that outlasted any single teacher. Quoting the artist and zoologist Jonathan Kingdon, who joined the faculty in 1959, it describes being a Makererean in the early 1960s as belonging at once to "a very local, indigenous institution" and to a "global, Uhuru independence movement."

## After Trowell

Cecil Todd replaced Trowell in 1958. The Short Century describes him as a perfectionist who insisted that students master European conventions of drawing, pictorial construction and colour theory. Elimo Njau, who shared Trowell's belief in an African aesthetic, objected, as quoted in the same account: "Todd was blanketing our history, which was not his duty." Maloba, by contrast, argued against a search for a purely traditional culture, writing: "Are coffee trees and the radio not existing happily side by side with matoke [green banana] just now!" The arguments between the two camps, over whether East African art should draw on local tradition, on the wider world, or on both, ran through Makerere in the 1960s and have not gone away.

## Carrying the model outward

Until 1965, The Short Century notes, Makerere offered the only route to a university education in fine art for Kenyans. When Kenya's own university departments began, Makerere graduates ran them. Maloba, one of Trowell's first students, returned to Kenya in 1966 and, with Louis Mwaniki, set up a Department of Fine Art at the University of Nairobi. In 1972 the department moved to Kenyatta University, where Maloba was chair until 1974, when Mwaniki succeeded him. Njau, Eli Kyeyune and Musoke were among the non-Kenyan Makerere graduates who relocated to Nairobi.

A survey titled "Contemporary Artists in East Africa", by Judith von Daler Miller, found that nearly three-quarters of the established artists it discusses had attended or taught at the school. Its graduates, she wrote, "represent the Establishment of the art world." The school itself has kept changing. By 2014, The Short Century records, it had become a faculty and taken the name Margaret Trowell School of Industrial and Fine Arts.

## Why it matters now

Makerere-trained painters form part of the story told by the NCAI Collection, which includes work by Macua, Njau, Mulindwa, Musoke, Sempangi and Ntiro. Several appeared together in Mwili, Akili na Roho: Ten Figurative Painters from East Africa, shown at NCAI from October 2022 to January 2023. Seen together, their paintings do not resemble one another, which may be the school's most lasting result. Trowell's critics and defenders can agree that what she began produced independent artists. How much that independence owed to her methods, and how much to the students who resisted them, is a question the work itself keeps open.

title: A fountain and an antelope: Chemchemi, Paa ya Paa and Elimo Njau's Nairobi
standfirst: In the years around Kenya's independence, a South African writer and a Tanzanian-born painter built rooms in Nairobi where artists, poets and playwrights could work together. Two of them, Chemchemi and Paa ya Paa, still shape how the period is told.
bodyMarkdown:
Before Nairobi had a settled commercial gallery scene, it had a handful of rooms where artists and writers met. Two of them were founded within two years of each other in the early 1960s, and a single artist, Elimo Njau, connects them. Chemchemi, a word that means fountain in Kiswahili, opened in 1963. Paa ya Paa, which means "the antelope rises," followed in 1965. This essay looks at what each was, who gathered there, and why the story of artist-led space in Nairobi often begins with them.

## A sister to Mbari

The founder of Chemchemi was the South African writer Es'kia Mphahlele, then in exile. According to Wikipedia's account of his life, he arrived in Nairobi in August 1963, a few months before Kenya's independence in December. The idea came from the Congress for Cultural Freedom, whose executive director, John Hunt, proposed a centre modelled on the Mbari clubs of Nigeria. Within months, the account says, a warehouse was converted into offices, an auditorium for experimental theatre and music, and an art gallery.

Mphahlele described the new centre in the Journal of Modern African Studies in 1965. "Bang in the middle of a dialogue now going on about African culture ... Chemchemi Creative Centre has been born," he wrote. It came "as a sister to the three Mbari writers' and artists' clubs in Nigeria," he continued, and would be "inspired by the same aims, although the methods of achieving them will obviously be guided by local national conditions."

The centre's programme was broad. Mphahlele took charge of writing and theatre, running writers' workshops in the districts and touring drama groups to schools. NCAI's exhibition notes on Elimo Njau record that Njau founded Chemchemi in 1963 alongside Mphahlele, and the biography prepared for NCAI says he led the visual arts programme at the centre. The artist Asaph Ng'ethe Macua exhibited at Chemchemi in 1964, according to his NCAI biography.

The centre's funding later became a point of controversy. A study of Nairobi as a capital of African political exiles in the 1960s, hosted by Pitzer College, reports that Mphahlele said he had not known that institutions he directed, Chemchemi among them, were being financed in secret by the American Central Intelligence Agency through the Congress for Cultural Freedom. The same study credits Mphahlele's founding of Chemchemi with laying literary foundations in East Africa, saying its role "cannot be overestimated."

## Elimo Njau's path to Nairobi

Njau was born in 1932 in Tanzania, in a Lutheran mission family. The Short Century notes that his father was a first-generation convert and a teacher. Njau studied at the Margaret Trowell School at Makerere, and according to a biographical profile he lectured there from 1959 to 1962. In 1959 he painted a set of murals at St James and All Martyrs Cathedral in Murang'a, commissioned by the Anglican Church to honour civilians killed during the Mau Mau uprising. The Short Century observes that they set New Testament scenes in the landscape of central Kenya. In The Baptism of Christ, Jesus is baptised not in the Jordan but at the Chania waterfalls.

Njau was one of several Makerere graduates from outside Kenya who settled in Nairobi, and the Short Century dates his arrival to 1959. Once there, he worked among writers. The NCAI notes list Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Okot p'Bitek and Hilary Ng'weno among the contemporaries who spurred him on, and his biography prepared for NCAI adds Mphahlele and Jonathan Kariara among the writers and intellectuals he worked with.

## The antelope rises

In 1965 Njau and his wife, Phillda Njau, founded Paa ya Paa on Ridgeways Road. NCAI's exhibition notes say he established it with Pheroze Nowrojee and James Kangwana, among others. The Smithsonian Libraries' reading list on modern African art describes it as one of the handful of Nairobi cultural establishments at the centre of modern art in Kenya, and notes that it was more than a gallery: it organised children's art workshops, poetry readings and other cultural events.

A principle written into the place came from Njau's own teaching. The Short Century quotes a policy he formulated in 1963, published in the journal Transition: "Do not copy. Copying puts God to sleep." It adds that the phrase is displayed on a wall at Paa ya Paa. The Smithsonian Libraries describe it as Njau's favourite maxim, and an article by Johanna Agthe in the Journal of Religion in Africa connects it to a wider pattern in East African art, in which some artists develop personal philosophies of creativity grounded in religious belief.

The centre was also a venue. NCAI's biography of Jak Katarikawe lists a 1968 exhibition with Samuel Wanjau at Paa ya Paa Gallery among his group shows, and the Smithsonian Libraries entry for a 1993 survey essay places Njau and Paa ya Paa, together with Ruth Schaffner and Gallery Watatu, at the centre of what was happening on the non-tourist art scene. A survey of East African artists by Judith von Daler Miller notes that Njau had been co-director of two defunct galleries and was running three others at the time of writing.

Paa ya Paa also survived loss. A profile of Njau on the Daily Kenya blog says that a fire in 1997 hit the premises, and that he rebuilt them with an open-air gallery.

## What the two spaces had in common

Chemchemi and Paa ya Paa differed in origin. One was a branch of an international cultural programme with a foreign backer, led by a South African exile. The other was set up by an East African artist and his wife with local partners. Yet they shared a premise: that a city in the middle of a political transition needed somewhere for artists to show, argue and learn from each other, outside the classroom and outside the state.

The record that survives is uneven. Much of what we know about Chemchemi comes from Mphahlele's own accounts and from scholars of literature, and the Short Century itself says that the first generation of Kenyan artists have received less study than their achievements deserve. A fuller history of these rooms would need more of their own archives.

## Njau and NCAI

Elimo Njau is represented in the NCAI Collection by Dream Landscape (1968), an oil on canvas, and his work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili na Roho: Ten Figurative Painters from East Africa. The exhibition also included Macua, Katarikawe and others whose careers touched Chemchemi, Paa ya Paa or both. Njau's later reputation rests on a body of work but also on an idea he put into practice: that an artist might build the institution he or she needs.

title: The dealer and the village: Gallery Watatu, Ruth Schaffner and the Ngecha artists
standfirst: In the 1980s and 1990s a Nairobi gallery run by a Californian dealer became the route to market for self-taught painters from a village outside Limuru. The partnership made careers and drew criticism.
bodyMarkdown:
Ngecha is a village on the outskirts of Nairobi, near Limuru. In 1990 it gave its name to an exhibition at a gallery in the city centre, Ngecha: Village of Painters, listed in Sane Wadu's exhibition record at Gallery Watatu. The title captured something that had become hard to ignore. A large number of self-taught painters were working in and around the village, and most took their pictures to the same place. This essay looks at that gallery, its owner, and the artists who made their names through it.

## A gallery in the city

A Smithsonian archival record for a small collection of printed cards from Gallery Watatu includes a short institutional history. It says the gallery was founded in 1969 by the painters Robin Anderson and Yony Waite and the graphic designer David Hart, and was one of Nairobi's longest-established galleries. It stood in the central business district and was, the history says, the first in the area to show both international and local artists. In 1985 it was sold to Ruth Schaffner, a gallery owner from California, and her husband, the artefacts dealer Adama Diawara. The new owners, the history says, focused on cultivating contemporary Kenyan art. The gallery closed in 2011. Other accounts differ on details of the early years. A 2011 report in the Nation, for instance, dates the gallery to 1968 and credits Schaffner and Diawara as its founders, so the Smithsonian record is followed here.

Schaffner's name recurs in the biographies of the artists she championed. A Los Angeles Times obituary dated March 1996 notes that she owned and operated the Watatu Gallery in Nairobi, "where she encouraged young African artists." The Nation report, written years after her death, said her passing left nearly 150 artists based at the gallery without it. The Smithsonian Libraries' reading list on Kenyan art places Schaffner and her gallery, with Elimo Njau's Paa ya Paa, at the centre of the non-tourist art scene in the early 1990s.

Her role was not uncontested. A 2011 article in allAfrica reports that some artists, Etale Sukuro among them, believe that Schaffner held back the development of Kenyan art to a large extent. Both views, that she was a patron of young artists and that she shaped a market in ways that limited some, appear in the record.

## A painter takes his work to the gallery

The clearest case is Sane Wadu. Born Walter Njuguna Mbugua in 1954 in Nyathuna, he worked as a teacher and a civil servant before giving up both to experiment with painting in 1983, according to NCAI's exhibition notes. His first works, according to the Red Hill Art Gallery's biography, were experiments with household paint on plastic sheets and on his clothes. People around him called him insane, so he took the name Sane. He submitted his first paintings to Gallery Watatu in 1984. Red Hill writes that Schaffner "saw behind these rough and impetuous brush strokes the real talent as an artist."

Writing in Frieze in 2022, Eric Otieno Sumba noted that Wadu's practice had at first been seen as too challenging for Kenya's conservative audiences, and that he struggled to find shows, but that Schaffner supported him "from the start." Frieze quotes Wadu, in a 2010 interview with Polly Savage published in Making Art in Africa 1960-2010: "This is how I found my role, trying to express myself. My struggle to survive pushed me until I got to the light." One of the paintings from that early period, Bless This Our Daily Bread (1984), shows a bearded figure in prayer over loaves and fish, and opened I Hope So, Wadu's survey at NCAI in 2022, the institute's inaugural exhibition.

## Forming a village association

The painters of Ngecha organised themselves. Red Hill's biography says that at the beginning of the 1990s Wadu founded the Ngecha Artists' Association with a group of self-taught artists including Wanyu Brush and Chain Muhandi. NCAI's notes also list Wadu as a founding member in 1990. Frieze dates the association's co-founding to 1995 and describes it as a collective of forty members that provided support, training and opportunities to generations of artists in the village. Sources disagree on the date, and the discrepancy is worth keeping in view.

Among the artists named in NCAI's notes, Meek Gichugu is also listed as a founding member of the association in 1990. The Red Hill biography records that in 1991, aged 22, he was given a solo exhibition at Gallery Watatu, where most of the nearly ninety works on show were sold. His paintings put the familiar and the sinister side by side: exotic fruits, strange animals, distorted human figures and sexual symbols, in restrained mustard and ochre tones. In 1999 Gichugu moved to Paris with his family, and the record of his Kenyan career ends there.

John Njenga Wambu, born in Ngecha in 1966, began painting in 1991, according to NCAI's notes, encouraged by the success of young artists from his village. Like many others, he took his work to Gallery Watatu, where his first solo exhibition sold out. He showed there regularly until his death in 1997. His work moved from naive realism to surreal scenes with human-animal figures, then to a quieter style of earth tones in which ethereal figures emerge from the buds of plants. By 1993 it had reached a wider audience through a group exhibition of contemporary African art in Japan.

Chelenge Van Rampelberg, born in Kericho in 1961, began painting and sculpting in 1984 at workshops run by Gallery Watatu with the Ngecha Artist Association, according to the biography prepared for NCAI. She had her first exhibition in 1985. She is described in the same material as working mainly in wood, with semi-abstract carvings centred on women. The NCAI Collection holds more than 140 of her works.

## A wider circle

Watatu's artists were not all from Ngecha. Jak Katarikawe, who was born in Uganda and moved to Nairobi in 1981, is listed in NCAI's notes as having had solo exhibitions at Gallery Watatu in 1975, 1990 and 1994, and the NCAI biography calls him a principal artist of the gallery from 1984. Wadu's own exhibition record includes Gallery Watatu shows in 1989, 1990 and 1995.

When the gallery lost its owner, artists scattered. The 2011 Nation report says that some continued by working from independent studios in places including Banana Hill, Forest Road, Ngong Road, Ngecha and Naivasha. The same report describes an attempt that year to revive the gallery with an exhibition of work by Katarikawe, Wanyu Brush and Wadu.

## What the story tells us

The Watatu years show how a single venue could organise an art scene. Schaffner's gallery gave painters without formal training a place to show, a buyer's market, and a name, the "Watatu artists," as Red Hill calls the group. The Ngecha Artists' Association gave them a collective voice. The Frieze review of Wadu's survey describes the association as a support system for the village, and says the exhibition also served as a stocktaking of the Kenyan scene: it marked, the review suggests, how far the local art community had come. Whether a gallery's patronage helped or constrained the painters it promoted remains a matter on which those who knew them disagree. The work they made, now held in collections across Kenya and abroad, gives the question a continuing life.

title: Making art under Amin: Ugandan painters and sculptors in the 1970s
standfirst: Under Idi Amin, art supplies vanished, teachers left and some artists fled. Those who kept working found other materials, other subjects and other cities. A look at what the record shows of Jak Katarikawe, Kefa Sempangi, Fabian Mpagi and their contemporaries.
bodyMarkdown:
Idi Amin ruled Uganda from 1971 to 1979. For the artists of Makerere and Kampala, those years combined several pressures: a collapsing supply of materials, the departure of foreign teachers and students, a government that wanted art only on its own terms, and danger for anyone who drew attention. This essay draws on the published record to describe how some Ugandan artists responded. It is a partial account. Much of what happened in studios during the 1970s was never written down, and the artists discussed here are those about whom something reliable survives.

## A school in decline

The art historian Sunanda K. Sanyal, in a doctoral dissertation on two generations of Makerere artists summarised by the Smithsonian Libraries, divides the school's history at roughly 1970. The 1950s and 1960s, she writes, "were ones of growth and optimism, but the reputation of the Makerere school of art declined in the 1970s and 1980s." The divide, she says, also marked a decrease in European instructors and in non-Ugandan students, which she attributes to the political upheavals in Uganda from the 1970s. A new cohort nonetheless emerged in those years, among them Francis Nnaggenda, Godfrey Banadda and Pilkington Ssengendo.

The Short Century, a research project of the East African Art and Museum Network, describes the regime's attitude to art in blunt terms: "Amin valued art only insofar as it boosted his ego, commissioning portraits, as well as insignias and medals, from Makerere." For the 1975 Organisation of African Unity summit in Kampala, it adds, students and staff made art for the congress venues. The same account says that artists criticised the dictator through veiled messages.

## Making do

Scarcity changed how art was made. The Short Century notes that the government's persecution of South Asian traders, who imported art supplies, forced artists to look for other materials. Francis Nnaggenda, who took up a teaching post at Makerere in 1978, used reclaimed scrap metal, plastic, glass and wood. In the project's words, the scarcity "facilitated a return to indigenous knowledge for Nnaggenda and others like him. He carved with fabricated chisels, employed sap as a protective agent, and painted with coffee and mixtures of organic matter." Batik, long dismissed as kitsch, also found new favour, because "the cotton, dyes, and wax needed to produce it were cheap and readily available."

## Jak Katarikawe

Jak Katarikawe was born around 1940 in Kigezi, in southern Uganda. He had no formal art education. According to the biography prepared for NCAI, he cited his mother's wall paintings and the murals of the cathedral at Rushoroza as early influences, and his talent was recognised by David Cook, a lecturer in literature at Makerere. NCAI's exhibition notes add that he spent two years working under Sam Joseph Ntiro there, and list solo exhibitions at the Nommo Gallery in Kampala in 1969 and 1970.

After Amin took power, the NCAI biography says, Katarikawe withdrew to his rural home in Kigezi, and in 1981 he moved to Nairobi. His work nevertheless travelled during the decade. NCAI's notes list solo shows at the Commonwealth Institute in London and the African Heritage House in Nairobi in 1975, and a group appearance at FESTAC 77 in Lagos. His paintings, in the NCAI biography's description, are narrative and personal, merging folklore, erotic fantasy and everyday village life. Western critics called him the "East African Chagall." The Museum of World Cultures in Frankfurt holds more than 150 of his works. Katarikawe died in October 2018.

## Kefa Sempangi

Kefa Frederick Sempangi was born in Uganda in 1939. He studied fine art at the Margaret Trowell School and then at the Royal College of Art in London, graduating in 1970, and later took a doctorate in art history at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. He returned to lecture in art history at Makerere. His work was shown in Uganda and the UK, including at the Camden Art Centre in London in 1968 and 1969, and in the 1960s and 1970s his practice ranged across surrealist portraiture, abstraction, found-object assemblage and cast bronze, according to the NCAI biography.

The Short Century singles out his sculpture Omugerengejjo, which it says juxtaposes Christian imagery with objects of traditional divination, and uses it to illustrate how artists addressed the coexistence of religious and traditional beliefs. Sempangi's career was then interrupted. A Presbyterian church-history page states that Amin ordered him killed and that he had several narrow escapes. Other biographical sources say he and his family went into exile in 1974, in the Netherlands and the United States, an experience recounted in his book A Distant Grief, written with Barbara Thompson. He returned to Kampala in 1979, after Amin's fall. On his return he founded what became the Presbyterian Church in Uganda, and he later served in public office while keeping up a personal art practice. Works by him are rare. The NCAI Collection holds Reptile (1967), an oil on board.

## Theresa Musoke

Theresa Musoke, born in Kampala in 1944, enrolled at the Makerere art school in 1962, according to an essay on MoMA's post site. The same essay says she completed a public mural commission for Mary Stuart Hall between 1962 and 1965, took a diploma at the Royal College of Art in 1967, studied for an MFA at the University of Pennsylvania from 1970, returned to Uganda in 1972 and taught at Makerere for two years before moving to Kenya, where she taught at Kenyatta University. The NCAI biography adds that she lived in Nairobi from 1974 to 1996 and returned to Kampala in 1997. In 1965 she became the first woman artist to have a solo exhibition at the Uganda Museum. The Short Century, which lists her among the non-Kenyan Makerere graduates who relocated to Nairobi, dates her move to 1976, so sources differ by two years on when she left.

## Fabian Mpagi and Peter Mulindwa

Fabian Mpagi graduated from the Margaret Trowell School in 1976 and stayed on as a postgraduate and teaching assistant. In 1983 he received a scholarship to study in Florence. On his return, according to auction-house biographies, he went into political exile in Kenya and set up a studio. He won the Habitat Art Competition in 1987, which brought a four-month residency in Paris. In 1988 he went back to Uganda and soon became director of the Nommo Gallery in Kampala, leaving that post in 1998 to concentrate on his own work. He died in 2002. The NCAI Collection holds an untitled portrait of his mother and younger brother from 1977.

Peter Mulindwa, born in Bunyoro in 1943, studied painting at Makerere from 1967 to 1971 and returned for a master's degree from 1977, according to the Makerere Art Gallery. The gallery describes his use of pointillism and mythical figures, and says that in politically repressive periods he used religious and anecdotal subjects to express criticism indirectly. His master's work looked at the relationship between Christianity and the local religions of Toro, his native region, under the title Art in Toro: Magicology and Religion. An untitled painting of 1982 combines books, brushes and graduation gowns with cowry shells and mythical creatures, which the gallery reads as a sign that modern education and religion have not erased people's attachment to traditional belief. NCAI's collection holds fourteen of his oil paintings, among them Uganda Martyrs (1968) and The Owl Drums Death (1982).

## Veiled messages

The Short Century also discusses Josephine Alacu, whose paintings used allegory to criticise the dictatorship. It cites Broken Eggs (1980), which it says draws on Genesis alongside political suffering. These examples show a strategy common to the artists above: religious and mythical imagery, in which a second meaning could be read by those who looked for it. The paintings could be read as devotional works, and for some viewers as something else.

## Looking back

Amin's fall in 1979 did not end the difficulties. The Short Century dates the recovery of Uganda's art world to 1994 onwards, as artists returned from exile with fresh training. For the 1970s, the record is thin, scattered across collections in Frankfurt, Bayreuth and Kampala. Several of the artists here appear in NCAI's collection and were shown in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection, and Katarikawe, Musoke and Mulindwa in Mwili, Akili na Roho.

title: Rooms to work in: Kuona Trust, the GoDown and Nairobi's artist collectives, 1990s to 2010s
standfirst: After the galleries of the 1980s, Nairobi artists built workshops, trusts and collectives of their own. A short history of Kuona Trust, the GoDown Arts Centre, Banana Hill and Maasai Mbili, and of the donor money and dispute that shaped them.
bodyMarkdown:
By the mid-1990s the best-known places to show art in Nairobi included Gallery Watatu and Paa ya Paa, both discussed elsewhere in this series. What followed over the next two decades was a period of organisation. Artists, and the people who worked with them, set up trusts, studios, centres and collectives. Some lasted and some did not. This essay follows the best-documented of them: Kuona Trust, the GoDown Arts Centre, Banana Hill, and the Kibera collective Maasai Mbili. It relies on a small body of scholarship and on the institutions' own accounts, which do not always agree.

## Kuona Trust

Kuona Trust was founded in 1995 at the National Museum of Kenya, according to Mimeta, one of its partner organisations, which describes it as a not-for-profit organisation serving visual artists. The Kuona Artists Collective, which carries on its work, gives the date as June 5, 1995, in a post marking thirty years. The researcher Danielle de Lame, in a 2021 chapter on the Nairobi art market, dates it to 1996 and says it stood next to the museum before moving to an industrial zone and then to Hurlingham.

The organisation's growth depended on outside money. In an academic paper published in 2024 under the title The Rise and Fall of Kuona Trust, Craig Halliday lists among its donors the British Council, the Dutch embassy, Hivos, the Heinrich Boll Foundation, GTZ and the Ford Foundation, and argues that its operations became increasingly reliant on foreign donor funding, especially after 2000, "as local government support remained limited." He dates its move into the GoDown Arts Centre to 2000, although other sources date the GoDown itself to 2003. The sources do not reconcile the two.

Mimeta says Kuona has "worked with over one thousand five hundred artists giving them skills and opportunities to advance themselves while increasing the profile and role of the visual arts in Kenya," and that it moved to premises off Dennis Pritt Road in Kilimani in late 2008. Its residency programme, in Mimeta's description, selects two artists a year, who must exhibit their work, submit a report and donate a piece to the centre's collection.

In 2003 Kuona produced Thelathini: 30 Faces, 30 Facets of Contemporary Art in Kenya. The Smithsonian Libraries' reading list on modern African art describes it as a project "to introduce some of Kenya's finest artist to new audiences," with thirty artists chosen by a committee over three years. The list includes Sane Wadu, Meek Gichugu, Theresa Musoke, Gakunju Kaigwa, Francis Kahuri, Richard Kimathi, Morris Foit, Chelenge Van Rampelberg, John Njenga and Jak Katarikawe, several of whom appear in the other essays in this series.

Halliday describes a shift toward support for conceptual art and socially engaged themes, and calls the 2009 exhibition Stereotypes, which addressed ethnic tensions in Kenya, a pivotal moment. His account of the ending is blunt: after financial mismanagement Kuona Trust, he writes, ceased operations in 2016, "highlighting risks of donor dependency." The Kuona Artists Collective emerged in 2017, when former beneficiaries came together to sustain the community and continue supporting emerging artists.

## The GoDown

The GoDown Arts Centre opened in 2003 on Dunga Road in Nairobi's Industrial Area, in what the National Museums of Kenya describes as a former industrial warehouse. Joy Mboya, who co-founded it, told Princeton Alumni Weekly that she established it because "we do not have sufficient training opportunities for the arts sector." The same article says initial support came from the Ford Foundation, and describes it as the first, and now the largest, multidisciplinary space for the arts in East Africa. De Lame notes that Thelathini was launched at its opening.

The centre was not an artist collective in the narrow sense. It brought together visual art, music, theatre, dance and film under one roof, and ran training in what its website calls creative entrepreneurship. Its festival Nai Ni Who? took place in 2013 and engaged young people from different neighbourhoods of the city; Mboya and Garnette Oluoch-Olunya wrote about it in a 2017 special issue of the journal Critical Interventions devoted to Kenyan art worlds, according to the Smithsonian Libraries' summary. Princeton Alumni Weekly reports that the centre supports more than 500 artists a year and receives over 100,000 visitors, roughly half of them children and young adults.

## Studios and collectives

Kuona and the GoDown were organisations with boards, donors and staff. Alongside them, a more informal tier grew up.

Banana Hill, about ten kilometres from the city centre, was home to the Banana Hill Art Studio, founded by Shine Tani. De Lame dates it to 1993, while the Banana Hill Art Gallery's own account gives 1992 for a gallery founded by Rahab and Shine Tani; either way, it dates from the early 1990s. The Smithsonian Libraries summary of Margaretta Swigert-Gacheru's 2013 book Creating Contemporary African Art lists Banana Hill Art Studio and Masai Mbili among collectives that artists formed on their own initiative, as workshops and as networks.

Maasai Mbili was founded in 2001 by Otieno Gomba and Otieno Kota, according to the African Arts Heritage site. The pair began by selling hand-painted signs along Kibera Drive and secured a permanent art centre in 2003. The collective works in painting and sign-writing, teaches workshops to local children, and carried out a project called Art4Peace after the post-election violence of 2007 and 2008. The same source says some of its artists later moved to spaces including Kuona.

Swigert-Gacheru frames much of this through the Kiswahili term jua kali, which once described informally trained artisans, and which she extends to artists and their networks. She argues that recycling and refuse became a common material for artists who lacked the means to buy expensive supplies.

Some ventures were short-lived. De Lame lists the Rahimtulla Museum of Modern Art, founded by Mary Collis and Carol Lees in the late 1990s and closed in 2009, and One Off Gallery, which Lees ran from her property off Limuru Road. The Dust Depot Art Studio, which Patrick Mukabi started near the Railway Museum, belongs to a later moment: de Lame dates it to 2015. Her chapter also mentions Msanii, a quarterly magazine that documented the scene from 2002 to 2009.

## What the pattern shows

Seen together, these places answer a question that earlier institutions had left open: where can an artist work, and who will pay for it? Commercial galleries such as Watatu sold work. The new organisations offered space, training, residencies and a kind of collective visibility, and several depended heavily on donors, a dependence that Halliday's history of Kuona identifies as a risk. The collective that replaced it began again from the artists up.

The record has gaps. Dates differ between sources, several organisations were documented mainly by those who ran them, and the artists' own voices are underrepresented. Anyone using this history should treat the years given above as the best available rather than settled. What the sources do show, taken together, is how many such places were founded between 1990 and 2015.

NCAI's collection holds work by several artists included in Thelathini, among them Gakunju Kaigwa, Francis Kahuri, Richard Kimathi, Morris Foit, Chelenge Van Rampelberg, Meek Gichugu and John Njenga. Many of them were shown in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
